items.summary: MONEO ERP exposes the Ping method of its _slave JSON-RPC service over WebSocket as @rpc.openpublic, so it can be called without a valid session. The method's only guard compares the calling application name with "_login", but that value is taken from the client-controlled params.appname field of the request. When the check passes, Ping stores an attacker-chosen session ID, user number and company in the server session store, and subsequent session validation accepts that session. An unauthenticated remote attacker can therefore create a valid session as any user, including administrators, in any company (tenant) hosted on the server and invoke authenticated RPC methods with that user's privileges, gaining read and write access to that company's data.

items.summary: In Eclipse Krazo Extensions up to and including 3.0.0, AsciiDocViewEngine passes MVC model values to Asciidoctor as document attributes without encoding them. Asciidoctor substitutes attribute references after it escapes HTML special characters and before it processes inline macros. As a result, attacker-controlled model values end up in the output as raw HTML and can inject AsciiDoc inline macros. This allows cross-site scripting in applications that render untrusted data through AsciiDoc views.

items.summary: The country manager page of the JTL-Shop administration backend (/admin/countries) writes the request parameter activeSortOrder without output encoding into a single-quoted JavaScript string and into HTML attributes. The overview page requires no CSRF token. An unauthenticated remote attacker can thereby cause script code to be executed in the browser of a logged-in backend user who opens a crafted link in the same browser (the session cookie carries no SameSite attribute by default); the code runs with the privileges of that user and can use the backend token of the same page to send requests to the backend. Visitors and customers are not affected.

items.summary: The access rules of JTL-Shop (export/.htaccess and export/backup/.htaccess) release files with the extensions gz and zip for the export directory without withdrawing this release in the subdirectory export/backup, in which the shop stores database dumps and file backups. As a result, backup files in this directory can be downloaded without authentication by anyone who knows or guesses the file name. Up to version 5.5.5 the names of database backups consist only of a timestamp; from version 5.6.0 they contain a random component, which does not replace access control. The backups contain the complete shop database (customer data, orders, password hashes) and, for file backups, files of the shop. The access rules are only evaluated by Apache. On installations where another web server, for example nginx, delivers static files such as gz and zip directly (including nginx in front of Apache), the files remain accessible even with the corrected rules, unless the directory is blocked at server level.

items.summary: The OPC (OnPage Composer) start menu, which JTL-Shop shows to logged-in backend users on storefront pages, writes the current page identifier (which contains the search term on search pages) and further values into single-quoted JavaScript strings without escaping. A single quote in the search term terminates the string. An unauthenticated remote attacker can thereby cause script code to be executed in the browser of a backend user who opens a crafted link while logged in to the backend in the same browser; the code runs with the privileges of that user and can use the backend session token contained in the same script to send requests to the backend. Visitors and customers do not receive the start menu and are not affected.

items.summary: The backend language switch action (quick_change_language) of the JTL-Shop administration backend is executed without a CSRF token check, and the supplied language value is neither validated against the installed backend languages nor encoded on output. The value is stored in the session and in the account data of the administrator and rendered without output encoding in JavaScript strings and HTML attributes of backend pages. An unauthenticated remote attacker can thereby cause script code to be executed in the browser of a logged-in administrator who opens a crafted web page; the code can perform actions with the privileges of that administrator.

items.summary: A flaw was found in Flatpak’s flatpak-portal. When a sandboxed application invokes Spawn() and maps two different file descriptors to the same handle, dup2() can fail. Affected Flatpak versions do not handle that failure, so a file descriptor that was open inside flatpak-portal (commonly the unfiltered D-Bus session bus) can be passed into the subsandbox. A malicious or compromised Flatpak app with no special privileges can use this to escape the sandbox.

items.summary: A flaw was found in Flatpak’s flatpak-system-helper. When a system-wide app, runtime, or extension uses the extra-data mechanism and its apply_extra logic creates a deeply nested directory tree, permission canonicalization can fail (for example with EMFILE). Affected Flatpak versions can still report success without clearing setuid/setgid bits, leaving a setuid-root executable under /var/lib/flatpak. A local attacker who can install or update such content system-wide, or who can already execute code as a local user in cooperation with that content, can escalate privileges to root.

In a multi-participant (virtual) control plane where vault partitions share the runtime's Vault token, an authenticated participant can set a callback secret alias that escapes its own vault partition. The connector then reads secrets of other participants or of the runtime, such as STS client secrets or the encryption key, and sends them to an endpoint the attacker chooses.

items.summary:
Strong::Random versions through 0.96 for Perl allow every later rand output to be predicted from three earlier ones.

The generator keeps its state in a single number. Each call multiplies the state by a factor derived from it, and the returned digits encode that factor, so three consecutive outputs determine the state however the generator was seeded. Outputs are also biased: the first digit after the decimal point is never zero, so rand(256) never returns 1 to 24.

An attacker who sees three consecutive outputs can predict the tokens, passwords or key bytes that the same object later issues to other users.

items.summary: A flaw was found in ModemManager. When parsing a Cell Broadcast Message, some 3GPP data-coding-scheme values (8-bit and reserved character sets) are not handled. The process hits a reachable assertion and aborts. An attacker who can deliver a crafted Cell Broadcast PDU over the radio network, or via a modem AT channel, can cause ModemManager to exit. Repeated aborts can exhaust systemd's default start limit and leave the service failed.

items.summary: A vulnerability was found in Undertow where the ProxyProtocolReadListener reuses the same StringBuilder instance across multiple requests. This issue occurs when the parseProxyProtocolV1 method processes multiple requests on the same HTTP connection. As a result, different requests may share the same StringBuilder instance, potentially leading to information leakage between requests or responses. In some cases, a value from a previous request or response may be erroneously reused, which could lead to unintended data exposure. This issue primarily results in errors and connection termination but creates a risk of data leakage in multi-request environments.

The response headers and body were sent but the client would continue waiting as Undertow does not send the expected 0\r\n termination of the chunked response. This results in uncontrolled resource consumption, leaving the server side to a denial of service attack. This happens only with Java 17 TLSv1.3 scenarios.

items.summary: A vulnerability was found in Undertow. This issue requires enabling the learning-push handler in the server's config, which is disabled by default, leaving the maxAge config in the handler unconfigured. The default is -1, which makes the handler vulnerable. If someone overwrites that config, the server is not subject to the attack. The attacker needs to be able to reach the server with a normal HTTP request.

items.summary:
A vulnerability was found in Undertow. This vulnerability impacts a server that supports the wildfly-http-client protocol. Whenever a malicious user opens and closes a connection with the HTTP port of the server and then closes the connection immediately, the server will end with both memory and open file limits exhausted at some point, depending on the amount of memory available. 

At HTTP upgrade to remoting, the WriteTimeoutStreamSinkConduit leaks connections if RemotingConnection is closed by Remoting ServerConnectionOpenListener. Because the remoting connection originates in Undertow as part of the HTTP upgrade, there is an external layer to the remoting connection. This connection is unaware of the outermost layer when closing the connection during the connection opening procedure. Hence, the Undertow WriteTimeoutStreamSinkConduit is not notified of the closed connection in this scenario. Because WriteTimeoutStreamSinkConduit creates a timeout task, the whole dependency tree leaks via that task, which is added to XNIO WorkerThread. So, the workerThread points to the Undertow conduit, which contains the connections and causes the leak.
